Sultan Haidar Ali Datasheet as part of RadioLink for Team 105

Submission: 10, 26, 2026

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This datasheet documents the hub subsystem of RadioLink, Team 105's embedded project. It is written so the design can be reviewed on its own, without the team report open beside it.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text: RadioLink is a hub-and-spoke system, and this board is the hub. It has an on-board OLED for graphics, a debug LED, and three UART ports. Board 1 carries the microphone, board 2 carries the pushbuttons and a temperature sensor, and board 3 carries the speaker. The microphone and button boards send their data to the hub. The hub shows a custom interface on the OLED, which is navigated with board 2's buttons, and it plays the microphone signal through the speaker.

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text:
My work on RadioLink has centered on concept ideation, user-needs benchmarking, and the hub itself. The hub receives the microphone and temperature data, presents it on a custom OLED interface that is navigated with the pushbuttons, and sends the microphone signal to the speaker.

  • Block Diagram
  • Component Selection
  • Bill of Materials
  • Schematic
  • Power Budget

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This block diagram is the hub subsystem of RadioLink, Team 105's hub-and-spoke design. A Microchip PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano sits at the center. A computer supplies 5 V over USB. An ST L7805CV provides the regulated 5 V rail from the 9 V input. A Microchip MCP1700-3302E/TO makes 3.3 V from that 5 V rail for the display. The MCP1700 is rated for 250 mA. The drawing below still prints 500 mA on the 3.3 V rail, which was the placeholder before this part was selected.

The microcontroller drives an EastRising ER-OLED0.96-1.3W over I2C. That module is a 128 x 64 panel with an SSD1306 controller. It is not a UG-2864HSWEG01. SDA is RB2 and SCL is RB1, after the 2N7000G level shifters. The OLED side of that bus is 3.3 V, and the microcontroller side is 5 V. A red LED is driven from RA2 using PWM. The module is the intentional exception to the through-hole preference.

Three UART ports connect this hub to the other boards. Each link is 5 V and uses an RX/TX pair:

  • Connector 1: RX on RC3, TX on RC2
  • Connector 2: RX on RF1, TX on RF0
  • Connector 3: RX on RA4, TX on RA3

These ports connect to the microphone board, the button and temperature board, and the speaker board. The microphone and button boards send data in. The hub shows temperature readings and the audio path on the OLED, and it sends the microphone signal out to the speaker.

docs.text: Figure 1: Hub block diagram for RadioLink. The drawing still labels the 3.3 V regulator as 500 mA. The selected 3.3 V part is the MCP1700-3302E/TO, rated 250 mA.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text:
The hub PCB is meant to be assembled, soldered, inspected, and repaired by hand. Through-hole packages are preferred wherever they are practical. The OLED module is an intentional exception, because that display assembly is not a discrete through-hole part.

Four parts were selected against that rule: the display module, the 9 V to 5 V regulator, the I2C level-shift MOSFETs, and the 5 V to 3.3 V regulator. SSD1306 is the controller inside the display. It is not the orderable module.

docs.title: OLED Display
docs.text:
Requirements: A readable graphic display for the hub UI, small enough for this board, with an I2C interface the PIC18F57Q43 can drive. Logic supply must work from the 3.3 V rail. The module may be a flex-connected assembly. It does not have to be through-hole.

SSD1306 names the controller IC. The orderable part is the EastRising module that uses that controller.

docs.title: Option 1: DLC-D1.54AGW#1
docs.text:
• $18.69 each
  • Link to product
Pros Cons 128 x 64 resolution 16-week lead time Large 1.54-inch display Requires 1 KB framebuffer Common SSD1309 controller Panel assembly, not a through-hole part Open-source drivers available Different controller from the selected module

docs.title: Option 2: DLC-D2.23AGW#1
docs.text:
• $25.40 each
  • Link to product
Pros Cons Large 2.23-inch display Fewer SSD1305 libraries available Easy to read Requires 12.5 V VCC Only 512 bytes of PIC RAM for framebuffer More expensive Only 128 x 32 resolution Panel assembly, not a through-hole part

docs.title: Option 3: ER-OLED0.96-1.3W
docs.text:
• $2.49 each
  • Link to product
  • Series datasheet

This is an EastRising 0.96-inch, 128 x 64, white OLED module with a top-contact FPC. The controller on the module is an SSD1306. The module is not a breakout board and it is not the UG-2864HSWEG01 drawn on the current schematic. That is a different orderable display that also uses an SSD1306.

EastRising lists VDD as 1.65 V to 3.3 V, typical 2.8 V. Logic-high is 0.8 x VDD. With the internal charge pump enabled, VBAT is specified as 3.5 V to 4.2 V. IDD is 180 µA typical and 300 µA maximum. With the charge pump generating VCC, IBAT at 100% of the pixels on is 25.6 mA typical and 32.0 mA maximum (datasheet Note 8: VDD = 2.8 V, generated VCC = 7.25 V). The framebuffer is 128 x 64 bits, which is 1 KB.

Pros Cons SSD1306 controller, with I2C available on this module 0.96-inch screen is small 128 x 64 FPC assembly, not through-hole $2.49, and it was available to order 1 KB framebuffer Logic supply accepts 3.3 V Charge-pump VBAT minimum in the datasheet is 3.5 V. Verify operation from the 3.3 V rail.

Choice: ER-OLED0.96-1.3W

Rationale: The hub UI only has to show temperature and audio status. A 128 x 64 SSD1306 module does that, costs $2.49, and does not have the 12- and 16-week lead times of the larger panels. Option 2 also needs 12.5 V, which this board does not have. The FPC module is the intentional exception to the through-hole preference.

The current schematic symbol is still labeled UG-2864HSWEG01. That label is not this module. The KiCad symbol still has to be changed. See the schematic page.

docs.title: 9 V to 5 V Regulator
docs.text:
Requirements: Make a regulated 5 V rail from the 9 V barrel jack for the Curiosity Nano, the debug LED, and the current that the 3.3 V regulator draws. The package should be through-hole. The part must stay in regulation at 9 V and at the budgeted load, and the heat has to be acceptable without treating the regulator as an efficient converter.

The generic name "7805" is the 5 V family. The orderable part selected here is the STMicroelectronics L7805CV, which is the TO-220 single-gauge version of the L7805C.

docs.title: Option 1: L7805CV (STMicroelectronics)
docs.text:
• ~$1.08 each
  • Link to product
  • ST L78 datasheet
Pros Cons Fixed 5 V, TO-220, through-hole Linear regulator: the drop from 9 V to 5 V becomes heat Output current up to 1.5 A Quiescent current up to 8 mA at 25 °C 9 V is inside the 7 V to 18 V test range used for the 5 V specification up to 1 A Minimum load for regulation is 5 mA Datasheet test circuit uses 0.33 µF in and 0.1 µF out, which is what the schematic already has (C9, C10) Dropout is typically 2 V at 1 A and 25 °C, so it is not a low-dropout part

docs.title: Option 2: MCP1702T-5002E/CB (Microchip)
docs.text:
• ~$0.65 each
  • Link to product
Pros Cons Very low quiescent current 250 mA maximum output Good for battery operation SOT-23, not through-hole Accepts up to 13.2 V input Less common than the 7805 family High DigiKey stock

This option is a 5.0 V LDO. It is not the 3.3 V regulator selected later.

docs.title: Option 3: MC7805CDTRKG (onsemi)
docs.text:
• ~$0.49 each
  • Link to product
Pros Cons Same 7805 family, 5 V output Linear, so it also dissipates (9 V − 5 V) × Iout Low cost DPAK, not through-hole Up to 1 A output Harder to hand solder than TO-220

Choice: L7805CV

Rationale: The budgeted 5 V current, after the 25% margin, is 71.625 mA. That is far under 1.5 A, and it is above the 5 mA minimum load. At 9 V in, the headroom above 5 V is 4 V, which is more than the typical 2 V dropout at 1 A.

Dissipation at that margined output current, plus the 8 mA maximum quiescent current, is:

P = (9 V − 5 V) × 0.071625 A + 9 V × 0.008 A = 0.359 W

TO-220 junction-to-ambient thermal resistance in the ST datasheet is 50 °C/W, so the rise is about 18 °C. A heatsink is not required at this load. The efficiency is about 50% at this current, because a linear regulator turns the extra input voltage into heat. Simplicity is not the same thing as efficiency. The TO-220 package is why this part won over the smaller 7805 and the MCP1702.

docs.title: I2C Level-Shift MOSFET
docs.text:
Requirements: SDA and SCL have to cross between the 5 V PIC pins and the 3.3 V OLED pins. The translator has to be bidirectional, because I2C is open-drain. Two channels are required, one for SDA and one for SCL. The MOSFET should be N-channel, enhancement-mode, and through-hole. I2C current is set by the 10 kΩ pull-ups already on the schematic, so the channel current is well under 1 mA.

The circuit is the MOSFET level shifter used on the Adafruit monochrome OLED breakout: gate tied to the low-voltage rail, source on the low-voltage bus, drain on the high-voltage bus. The low side is 3.3 V. The high side is 5 V.

docs.title: Option 1: BSS138, as drawn on the current schematic
docs.text: Pros Cons N-channel MOSFET already used in this topology SOT-23, not through-hole Two devices are already placed as Q1 and Q2 Not pin-compatible with a TO-92 2N7000 Exact gate threshold depends on which BSS138 manufacturer is fitted. That manufacturer was not recorded.

docs.title: Option 2: onsemi 2N7000G
docs.text:
• TO-92, Pb-free 2N7000
  • onsemi 2N7000 datasheet
Pros Cons N-channel enhancement MOSFET in TO-92 VGS(th) is 0.8 V minimum and 3.0 V maximum at VDS = VGS and ID = 1 mA VDSS 60 V, continuous ID 200 mA RDS(on) is specified at VGS = 4.5 V and 10 V, not at 3.3 V Body diode and gate connection match the level-shifter topology A worst-case 3.0 V threshold on a 3.3 V gate has to be checked on the bench Two parts cover SDA and SCL Pinout is not the BSS138 pinout

onsemi Style 22 numbers the TO-92 pins as pin 1 source, pin 2 gate, pin 3 drain. The PCB symbol, footprint, and routing have to follow that datasheet. Do not reuse the BSS138 footprint.

docs.title: Option 3: 2N7002
docs.text:
Pros Cons Same 2N7000 electrical family, so the level-shifter discussion still applies SOT-23, which loses the reason for leaving the BSS138 Still not a drop-in for the current BSS138 footprint without a footprint check

Choice: two onsemi 2N7000G, Q1 and Q2

Rationale: Each I2C line needs its own MOSFET. The 2N7000G is selected because it is an N-channel enhancement MOSFET in TO-92 and the I2C current is tiny next to its 200 mA rating. In the shifter, the source connects to the 3.3 V side, the drain connects to the 5 V side, and the gate connects to 3.3 V.

It is electrically plausible for this current, and it is not guaranteed by the datasheet at the worst-case threshold. VGS(th) can be as high as 3.0 V, and the gate supply is 3.3 V. Verify that a worst-case part still pulls the 5 V side down through the 10 kΩ pull-ups. BSS138 and 2N7000G are not drop-in replacements.

docs.title: 5 V to 3.3 V Regulator
docs.text:
Requirements: A second regulator, separate from the L7805CV, has to make 3.3 V from the 5 V rail for the OLED. It needs a fixed 3.3 V output, a through-hole package, and enough current for the display. The load used here is the EastRising maximum of 32.0 mA IBAT plus 0.3 mA IDD, which is 32.3 mA, with the charge-pump caveat in the power budget.

This is not the 9 V to 5 V regulator.

docs.title: Option 1: Unlabeled 5-pin regulator on the current schematic
docs.text:
The schematic draws U2 as a 5-pin device with IN, EN, GND, OUT, and a pad pin. No manufacturer part number is on the sheet. The block diagram called this rail 500 mA. That rating was not tied to an orderable part.

Pros Cons Already drawn SOT-23-style package, not through-hole Has an enable pin MPN is unknown, so current, dropout, and capacitors cannot be checked 500 mA on the block diagram is not a datasheet rating

docs.title: Option 2: Microchip MCP1700-3302E/TO
docs.text:
• Fixed 3.3 V, TO-92
  • Microchip MCP1700 datasheet
Pros Cons Through-hole TO-92 No enable pin, so the current 5-pin symbol cannot be reused 250 mA maximum for a 3.3 V output Input is only specified up to 6.0 V, so it must run from 5 V, not from 9 V Input range 2.3 V to 6.0 V Typical quiescent current 1.6 µA, maximum 4 µA Stable with a 1.0 µF output capacitor, ESR 0 Ω to 2.0 Ω

TO-92 pin numbers in the Microchip pin table are pin 1 GND, pin 2 VIN, pin 3 VOUT. Dropout at 250 mA is 178 mV typical and 350 mV maximum for VR above 2.5 V. The 5 V input is 1.7 V above 3.3 V, which is above that dropout.

Junction-to-ambient thermal resistance for the TO-92 package in the datasheet is 92 °C/W. At 32.3 mA the dissipation is (5.0 V − 3.3 V) × 0.0323 A = 0.0549 W, about a 5 °C rise.

docs.title: Option 3: Microchip MCP1700T-3302E/TT
docs.text:
Pros Cons Same MCP1700 electrical limits, including 3.3 V and 250 mA SOT-23, not through-hole Same capacitor requirements Different pin order from the TO-92 part

Choice: MCP1700-3302E/TO

Rationale: 32.3 mA is a small fraction of 250 mA, and the TO-92 package matches the hand-assembly goal. The SOT-23 version of the same regulator was rejected for the package. The unlabeled 5-pin part was rejected because it has no orderable number and it is not through-hole.

The schematic already has 10 µF capacitors at C1 and C2 around this regulator. Microchip requires at least 1.0 µF on the output, with ESR from 0 Ω to 2.0 Ω, and about 1 µF on the input for loads up to 100 mA. Larger input capacitance is allowed. A 10 µF capacitor meets the minimum. It is acceptable only if its ESR is inside 0 Ω to 2.0 Ω. The schematic does not state the dielectric. Verify that C1 and C2 are low-ESR parts, such as ceramic, before treating 10 µF as a finished MCP1700 design. The capacitance value does not have to change.

docs.title: MCC Configuration
docs.text:
The hub uses the PIC18F57Q43 on the Curiosity Nano. The clock is the internal HFINTOSC. There is no external crystal on the schematic. Peripheral pin select maps the digital pins below.

Function Peripheral Pins System clock HFINTOSC Internal OLED I2C, after the 2N7000G shifters I2C SDA on RB2, SCL on RB1 Debug LED PWM RA2 UART connector 1 UART TX on RC2, RX on RC3 UART connector 2 UART TX on RF0, RX on RF1 UART connector 3 UART TX on RA3, RX on RA4 Debug button GPIO input SW1. The schematic does not label which PIC pin it uses.

The three UART ports are the links to the microphone board, the button and temperature board, and the speaker board. The block diagram does not assign a connector number to a specific board, so this table does not either. I2C is shifted from 5 V at the microcontroller to 3.3 V at the OLED by Q1 and Q2. SW1 is the debug button on this board, not the user buttons on board 2.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This schematic is the hub subsystem of RadioLink for Team 105. It is centered on a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano. The hub reads the microphone board and the button and temperature board over UART, shows that information on the EastRising ER-OLED0.96-1.3W, sends the microphone signal to the speaker board, and drives a local debug LED.

Power comes from a 9 V barrel jack. A 1 A fuse feeds an ST L7805CV, which regulates that input to 5 V. A Microchip MCP1700-3302E/TO makes 3.3 V from that 5 V rail for the display. Two onsemi 2N7000G MOSFETs, Q1 and Q2, translate SDA and SCL between the 5 V microcontroller and the 3.3 V display. The display module uses an SSD1306 controller. Test points, a pushbutton, and the red LED provide debugging access on the microcontroller side. Three 8-pin connectors carry the UART links to the other subsystems.

The board is intended to use through-hole parts where that is practical. The OLED module is the exception.

TODO, ECAD not updated. Figure 1, the PDF, and the KiCad zip are still the 2026-10-19 export. That export shows UG-2864HSWEG01 at U1, BSS138 at Q1 and Q2, and a 5-pin U2 with an enable pin. Do not treat the image as already containing the 2N7000G or the MCP1700-3302E/TO. The KiCad project was not edited, because the symbol pins and footprints cannot be swapped safely without checking ERC. These edits still have to be done in KiCad:

  • Replace the U1 symbol label with the ER-OLED0.96-1.3W module. Do not treat it as a UG-2864HSWEG01.
  • Replace Q1 and Q2 with onsemi 2N7000G, TO-92. Pin 1 is source, pin 2 is gate, pin 3 is drain. Source goes to the 3.3 V I2C side, drain goes to the 5 V I2C side, and gate goes to 3.3 V. Do not reuse the BSS138 footprint.
  • Replace U2 with MCP1700-3302E/TO, TO-92. Pin 1 is GND, pin 2 is VIN, pin 3 is VOUT. This part has no enable pin, so the EN net on the current symbol has to be removed rather than left floating.
  • Keep C1 and C2 at 10 µF only after checking that their ESR is between 0 Ω and 2.0 Ω.

Figure 1: Current hub schematic export. It still shows the previous OLED symbol, BSS138 level shifters, and the unlabeled 5-pin 3.3 V regulator. The intended parts are the ER-OLED0.96-1.3W, two 2N7000G devices, the L7805CV, and the MCP1700-3302E/TO.

docs.title: Function
docs.text:
RadioLink needs one board that can take the microphone and the button and temperature data, show it, and pass the microphone audio to the speaker. This schematic is that board.

The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano is the controller. Three UART connectors are the links to the other boards. One brings in the microphone, one brings in the pushbuttons and the temperature reading, and one carries the microphone signal out to the speaker. The connectors are logic-level RX and TX. They do not feed power to those boards, so the speaker amplifier is not a load on this schematic.

The ER-OLED0.96-1.3W is the interface the user sees. Board 2's buttons move through that screen. The module's SSD1306 logic is a 3.3 V interface, and the microcontroller I2C pins are 5 V, so Q1 and Q2 level-shift SDA and SCL. JP1 opens the display supply so the OLED can be powered down without shutting off the hub.

The 9 V barrel jack, the 1 A fuse, and the L7805CV make the 5 V rail for the microcontroller, the debug LED, and the UART logic. U2, the MCP1700-3302E/TO, makes the 3.3 V rail for the OLED from that 5 V rail. The red LED and SW1 are debug parts on this board. They are not the user controls. Those controls stay on board 2.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This budget is for the RadioLink hub only. It covers the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, the EastRising ER-OLED0.96-1.3W, the debug LED, the L7805CV, and the MCP1700-3302E/TO. The microphone, button, and speaker boards are not included. Their UART links are logic-level signals, and those boards carry their own supplies.

The 9 V barrel jack feeds the L7805CV. The 5 V rail feeds the PIC, the debug LED, and the MCP1700. The 3.3 V rail feeds the display. A linear regulator does not remove the load current. The MCP1700 input current is still a load on the 5 V rail, and that 5 V current is still a load on the 9 V input.

Currents below are datasheet limits or the allowances already used on this page. They are not lab measurements. The 25% margin is kept on each regulated rail. Quiescent current is included where the datasheet maximum is large enough to matter.

docs.title: Display current
docs.text:
The orderable display is the ER-OLED0.96-1.3W. SSD1306 is the controller on that module. EastRising Note 8 lists a maximum IBAT of 32.0 mA with the internal charge pump, VDD = 2.8 V, generated VCC = 7.25 V, and 100% of the pixels on. IDD maximum is 300 µA. Those two maxima add to:

32.0 mA + 0.3 mA = 32.3 mA

The same datasheet lists VBAT as 3.5 V to 4.2 V when the internal DC/DC is enabled, and VDD as 1.65 V to 3.3 V. This board's display rail is 3.3 V, which is the top of the VDD range and below the stated VBAT minimum. Verify the current with VDD and VBAT both at 3.3 V. The older 33 mA figure is not used. 32.3 mA is the sum of the published maxima, not a measurement at 3.3 V.

docs.title: Rails
docs.text:
Figure 1: Loads on the 5 V rail and the 3.3 V rail, including the 25% margin.

Figure 2: Current drawn from the 9 V barrel jack, including L7805CV quiescent current.

docs.title: 3.3 V rail
docs.text:
The only 3.3 V load in this budget is the display, at 32.3 mA.

Margined current = 32.3 mA × 1.25 = 40.375 mA

The MCP1700-3302E/TO is rated for 250 mA when the output is 2.5 V or higher. Remaining capacity is 250 mA − 40.375 mA = 209.625 mA.

Load power and regulator loss at the 32.3 mA datasheet sum, not at the margin, are:

P_load = 3.3 V × 0.0323 A = 0.1066 W

P_MCP1700 = (5.0 V − 3.3 V) × 0.0323 A = 0.0549 W

P_input ≈ 5.0 V × 0.0323 A + 5.0 V × 4 µA = 0.1615 W

The 4 µA term is the MCP1700 maximum quiescent current. It does not change the milliamp total. TO-92 thermal resistance in the MCP1700 datasheet is 92 °C/W, so 0.0549 W is about a 5 °C rise.

docs.title: 5 V rail
docs.text:
Load Current PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano allowance 15 mA Debug LED allowance, D4 with R7 = 330 Ω 10 mA MCP1700 input, equal to the 32.3 mA display current 32.3 mA Subtotal 57.3 mA After 25% margin 71.625 mA

The 15 mA PIC number is an operating allowance for 5 V operation with UART, I2C, and PWM. It is not a copied datasheet maximum and it is not a lab measurement. The 10 mA LED number is the existing allowance from (5 V − 1.8 V) / 330 Ω, rounded up. The 1.8 V LED drop was not taken from a datasheet for D4. Verify that LED forward voltage.

The L7805CV can supply up to 1.5 A. Remaining capacity against that rating is 1.5 A − 71.625 mA = 1.428 A. The 1 A fuse is on the 9 V input, not on the 5 V output.

At the margined 71.625 mA output current, using the L7805C maximum quiescent current of 8 mA at 25 °C:

P_L7805 = (9 V − 5 V) × 0.071625 A + 9 V × 0.008 A = 0.359 W

TO-220 junction-to-ambient thermal resistance in the ST L78 datasheet is 50 °C/W, so the rise is about 18 °C. Output power is 5 V × 0.071625 A = 0.358 W. Input power is 9 V × (0.071625 A + 0.008 A) = 0.717 W. Efficiency is 0.358 / 0.717 = 50%. The L7805CV is appropriate because the heat is small, not because a linear drop from 9 V to 5 V is efficient.

docs.title: 9 V input
docs.text:
Current from the barrel jack is the margined 5 V output current plus the 8 mA quiescent maximum:

71.625 mA + 8 mA = 79.625 mA

The fuse is 1 A, so the unused current is 1000 mA − 79.625 mA = 920.375 mA. That spare current is not a reason to power the speaker from this board. The speaker amplifier belongs on board 3.

A 500 mAh 9 V alkaline cell is not on the schematic. If one replaced the barrel jack, life at 79.625 mA would be 500 mAh / 79.625 mA = 6.28 hours. USB on the Curiosity Nano can power the microcontroller during programming, and that path is separate from this 9 V budget.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
The margined hub load is 71.625 mA on the 5 V rail and 40.375 mA on the 3.3 V rail. Both are far below the L7805CV 1.5 A rating and the MCP1700 250 mA rating. L7805CV dissipation at the margined load is 0.359 W. MCP1700 dissipation at the 32.3 mA display sum is 0.0549 W. The 9 V input, limited by the 1 A fuse, still has 920 mA of spare current.

The display number still needs a bench check, because the 32.0 mA IBAT maximum is specified for the charge pump at VDD = 2.8 V, and this rail is 3.3 V.
